cosy-lesson.title: "The only true wisdom is in knowing you know nothing.": Socrates

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Intellectual humility – a conscious awareness of the limitations of one's own knowledge.

p.em: Example: Embracing intellectual humility is the first step toward genuine learning.

cosy-blockquote.p: Preconceptions – opinions or ideas formed beforehand without adequate evidence or experience.

p.em: Example: Socratic questioning forces us to strip away our comfortable preconceptions.

cosy-blockquote.p: Ignorance – lack of knowledge, information, or awareness.

p.em: Example: Socrates argued that recognizing your own ignorance is the beginning of true wisdom.

cosy-blockquote.p: Dogmatism – the arrogant assertion of opinions as truths without proof or open-mindedness.

p.em: Example: Socrates challenged the dogmatism of local politicians who pretended to know everything.

cosy-blockquote.p: Paradox – a seemingly absurd or self-contradictory statement that actually reveals a deep truth.

p.em: Example: The Socratic paradox-that we know nothing-proves that real wisdom is self-awareness.

cosy-blockquote.p: Inquiry – a systematic investigation or the act of asking deep, searching questions.

p.em: Example: Through relentless inquiry, Socrates exposed the shallow arguments of his peers.

cosy-blockquote.p: Dialogue – a collaborative conversation aimed at uncovering truth rather than winning an argument.

p.em: Example: A Socratic dialogue requires active listening and a shared pursuit of clarity.

cosy-blockquote.p: Virtue – moral excellence, goodness, or the lived expression of high ethical standards.

p.em: Example: In ancient Athens, Socrates debated whether virtue could be taught or if it was innate.

cosy-blockquote.p: Cognizant – fully aware of or possessing conscious knowledge of something.

p.em: Example: Being cognizant of our own cognitive biases prevents us from making foolish assumptions.

cosy-blockquote.p: Contemplate – to think deeply and thoughtfully about philosophical or complex matters.

p.em: Example: He would often stand in the public square to contemplate the nature of justice.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
How does Socratic questioning help us dismantle our deeply held preconceptions about the world?
★ Complete using inversion: 'Seldom do we discover profound truths without active questioning.'

Why does modern social media encourage absolute dogmatism instead of intellectual openness?
★ How do you handle talking to someone who refuses to admit they could be wrong?

In what ways does possessing intellectual humility make a leader more effective and respected?
★ Is it easy for you to say "I don't know" when asked about a topic you aren't familiar with?

Why do we often fear admitting our ignorance, and how can we learn to view it as a positive starting point?
★ What is a subject where you are perfectly happy to remain ignorant?

How does the famous Socratic paradox-knowing that you know nothing-actually lead to real wisdom?
★ What is a paradox in your own life that you still find difficult to resolve?

Should modern education focus more on active inquiry rather than the passive memorization of facts?
★ What was the last topic that sparked a deep, personal inquiry in your spare time?

How can we revive the art of constructive dialogue in a world that is heavily polarized?
★ When was the last time you had a truly satisfying dialogue with someone who has opposite views?

Socrates believed that knowledge is virtue and that people only do bad things out of ignorance. Do you agree?
★ What is a personal virtue that you strive to protect no matter the external circumstances?

Why is it so difficult to remain cognizant of our own cognitive biases during heated debates?
★ Are you highly cognizant of how your emotions affect your logical arguments?

How can we find the quiet mental space to contemplate complex philosophical questions in a hyper-distracted world?
★ Where is your favorite place to go when you need to contemplate a major life decision?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: Discuss with your partner: Rank these types of minds from most to least wise, according to Socrates' philosophy: - 🧘 The Silent Contemplator Admits ignorance and quietly contemplates life's deep mysteries without arguing or lecturing others. - 🔍 The Passionate Inquirer Actively questions every social rule, authority, and traditional custom, seeking true, objective virtue. - 🎓 The Expert Specialist Possesses vast technical knowledge but remains completely dogmatic and narrow-minded outside their field. - 🤝 The Peaceful Diplomat Prefers harmonious dialogue and polite compromise over challenging others' preconceptions.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
In the future, advanced neural networks will scan our brains to identify and erase our hidden preconceptions. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you allow a machine to optimize your mind by clearing your biases?

As information becomes even more overwhelming, future societies will retreat into extreme dogmatism to survive. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Should schools teach children how to detect dogmatism in media from a young age?

Future artificial intelligence will display such perfect intellectual humility that humans will look arrogant in comparison. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Could you trust an AI doctor that openly admits it doesn't know the answer?

Our future reliance on algorithms will create a world of comfortable ignorance, where humans no longer understand how their technology works. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If technology managed everything, would you mind being ignorant of how it functions?

A future high-tech paradise will eliminate all struggle, but it will face the Socratic paradox of human boredom. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If you lived in a perfect world, how would you keep your life meaningful?

Future search engines will answer questions instantly, rendering the art of active human inquiry obsolete. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you miss the joy of searching for answers if everything were known instantly?

In the coming decades, virtual reality spaces will allow perfectly unbiased Socratic dialogue between historical enemies. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you participate in a global digital dialogue with strangers to solve world issues?

Future bio-engineering will allow us to physically upgrade human empathy, turning virtue into a biological guarantee rather than a choice. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you take a pill that guaranteed you would always act with perfect virtue?

We will eventually wear wearable sensors that make us dynamically cognizant of when we are being closed-minded. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ Would you wear a wristband that vibrated whenever you showed dogmatic thinking?

The hyper-accelerated future will leave absolutely no time to quietly contemplate the meaning of our existence. : Do you agree or disagree?
★ If life became twice as fast, how would you preserve your mental peace?

ul.li: Incorrect: I am more wise → Correct: I am wiser ((Short adjectives use comparative suffix '-er'))
Incorrect: Socrates was an expert of questioning → Correct: Socrates was an expert at questioning ((Use preposition 'at' after 'expert'))
Incorrect: The most of people think... → Correct: Most people think... ((Use 'Most people' for general statements))
Incorrect: If I was him, I would... → Correct: If I were him, I would... ((Subjunctive mood in conditional structures))
Incorrect: I am agree with you → Correct: I agree with you ((Agree is a verb and does not take the auxiliary 'am'))
